corrected_value.authors: Yang, J., Wang, S., Xu, Y., & Rayner, K.
corrected_value.title: Do chinese readers obtain preview benefit from word n+2? Evidence from eye movements.

decisions.location: Experiment 1, Discussion, page 18, lines 439-446; References, page 44, lines 1089-1091
decisions.quote:
Experiment 1 was an attempt to replicate Yang et al.’s findings, and the analyses on
the regions examined by Yang et al. (i.e., words n, n+1, and n+2) provided a full replication.
Consistent with their findings, we observed n+2 preview effects of 22ms on word n+2 in gaze
duration when word n+1 was high-frequency. Yang et al. (2009) found a marginal (p=0.051)
effect in gaze duration of 22ms, and no effect in other measures. Furthermore, Yang et al.
(2012) did not find any effect of the word n+2 preview when a low-frequency word n+1 was
used. Thus, the pattern of effects was replicated in the current experiment, and our results are
consistent with Yang et al.’s findings.
decisions.reason: Experiment 1 explicitly re-tests the positive word n+2 preview benefit reported in Experiment 2 of Yang, Wang, Xu, and Rayner (2009) (doi:10.1037/a0013554) using its 20 high-frequency word n+1 stimuli, analysed as an independent subset alongside the 20 low-frequency word n+1 stimuli from Yang, Rayner, Li, and Wang (2012) (shipped row input_row_index 1497, doi:10.1007/s11145-010-9282-7). Shipped row 1497 represents only the 2012 low-frequency follow-up study; Yang et al. (2009) is a separate original publication with different authors, stimuli, experimental condition, and empirical finding, so report equivalence does not apply.

corrected_value.authors: Cutter, M. G., Drieghe, D., & Liversedge, S. P.
corrected_value.title: Preview benefit in English spaced compounds.

decisions.quote:
However, we did hypothesise an interaction, such that
an n+2 preview effect would be observed in the idioms, but not the phrases. We made this
hypothesis on the basis that idioms may have multi-word unit representational status, such
that the first character of the idiom may licence the processing of the entire unit (idiom), thus
leading to the early extraction of information from word n+2. In contrast the first character of
a phrase should not licence the processing of a larger lexical unit (the phrase) and therefore
the early extraction of information from word n+2. In this way the second constituent of an
idiom would be processed in the parafovea despite the processing difficulty of the first
constituent, in a similar manner to the second constituent of a spaced compound in Cutter et
al.’s (2014) study. If this did occur, it would be strong evidence for the idioms being
parafoveally processed as a multi-word unit.
decisions.reason: Current Experiment2 prospectively tests Cutter2014specific multi-word-unit parafoveal preview finding: low-frequency first constituents should permit terminal preview when the unit is lexicalized. It contrasts idioms and matched phrases, reports the predicted interaction absent, and explicitly compares that result with spaced-compound preview benefits, discussing constituent predictability/transitional probability. This is an actual conceptual retest, despite the authors reserving an overall replication label for the Yangbenchmark in Experiment1. The empirical claim is not mere use of a reading task or interactive-activation theory. Current new observations come from80Chinese readers; Experiments1/2share that sample, not independent replications of each other. All shipped and corrected identities were checked:1497is Yang2010online/2012issue, and existing additional target0is Yang2009. Those papers concern the word-frequency preview benchmark, not these specific idiom/spaced-compound findings. The named original reports have distinct author/title, empirical stimulus-language/measure descriptions and directly attributed findings; no alternate-report equivalence is evidenced. They are not merely inferred independent because DOIs or years differ. The current authors directly compare each, rather than only citing an earlier ancestor through a later replication. One pair per named original, no outcome adjudicated. Original full-body/participant-overlap limits remain explicit, without inventing identical or independent people.
